newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Sears chief under pressure after sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sears chief under pressure after sale.

text.p: Struggling British retailer Sears Plc on Monday tried to placate disgruntled investors with the sale of its Freemans mail order arm plus the promise of a 410 million pound ($686 million) cash handout.
But analysts said embattled chief executive Liam Strong's job was still on the line for failing to revive the sprawling shoes-to-Selfridges retail empire after five years at the helm.
They said investors wanted more radical solutions, including ditching the struggling British Shoe Corporation or a possible demerger of Selfridges, the group's star profit performer.
Analysts said a growing number of institutional investors were baying for Strong's blood, but the lack of an obvious successor might give him a breathing space.
"There's little chance of him going until they've found an adequate successor," said one retail analyst who asked to remain anonymous.
One major investor, Philips & Drew Fund Management (PDFM), said it would keep an open mind on Sears management ahead of meetings with executives of the company later this week.
A spokeswoman for PDFM, which holds an 11.8 percent stake in Sears, said fund managers would make no further comment ahead of the meetings.
Strong's failure to deliver was highlighted last week when Sears warned that annual profits would be less than last year's 100.1 million pounds after a disappointing Christmas.
Strong, formerly marketing director at British Airways, was brought in in 1992 to transform the retail conglomerate.
Investor patience has worn thin as his efforts to shake up the group have not delivered profit growth and its shares, up 1/2p to 88-1/2 on Monday, are still underperforming.

The poor showing has prompted renewed calls for a break up of the group to realise value from the highly profitable Selfridges department store in London's West End and women's fashion chains such as Warehouse and Wallis.
Some retail analysts said even a break-up looked unattractive, pointing to the experience of Hanson Plc, whose demergers did not solve its share price underperformance.
"Sears' break-up valuation is not hugely more than the price now," said one retail analyst.

After selling Freemans, investors want Strong to take the knife to Sears' ailing British Shoe Corporation, which has seen sales fall nearly three percent so far in the second half of the current year in a difficult British footwear market.
"Our footwear trading performance over the next 12 months is crucial in terms of determining the potential of the footwear business for Sears," Strong said in a statement.
Industry sources said Sears could struggle to offload the business and any deal could mean a sizeable hit on the balance sheet, although BSC's property portfolio might be an attraction.
Footwear, with annual sales of up to 600 million pounds, has around 500 shops and concessions in some 250 department stores.

Strong has already introduced new formats with Shoe Express and Shoe City, but efforts to sell the unwanted stores were hampered last year when shops sold to privately-owned retailer Facia had to be taken back after Facia collapsed.

Strong also faces pressure to float Selfridges, which is valued at between 590 and 650 million pounds. But industry sources said there were no immediate plans to spin off what was the most profitable part of the group.
Sears said the sale of Freemans to Littlewoods Organisation for 395 million pounds ($664 million) in cash would bring savings of about four million pounds per year.

The group also said it was developing a structure to return cash to shareholders in some six months' time and expected to give further details in April. Analysts said Sears had yet to decide how to do this. ($1=.5974 Pound)
